title: The Claude Harness Pattern: Context, Memory, and Cognitive Scaffolding
thesis: The most effective Claude users aren't writing better prompts — they're building harnesses: layered systems of CLAUDE.md files, skills, hooks, and memory that turn a chat window into a persistent, self-improving agent. This pattern emerged independently across multiple creators and maps directly to how production AI systems are being architected.
why_it_matters: The gap between 'using Claude' and 'building with Claude' is exactly this pattern. Context engineering (what goes in the window), memory (what persists across sessions), and harness (the scaffold that orchestrates both) are three distinct disciplines. Most people conflate them. The entries in this dive show practitioners who figured out the distinction independently.
action_sketch:
1. Audit your current Claude setup — do you have a CLAUDE.md? Skills? Hooks?
2. Map your workflow: what context does Claude need every session vs. occasionally?
3. Build a minimal harness: CLAUDE.md (permanent rules) + primer.md (session state) + skills/ (reusable workflows)
4. Add memory persistence: file-based or MCP-backed cross-session recall
5. Layer in hooks for self-correction (caveman mode, token discipline, audit-after-step)
prerequisites: Claude Code or similar agent-mode tool

title: MediaPipe × TouchDesigner: Real-Time Body-to-Art Pipeline
thesis: MediaPipe's body/hand/face tracking combined with TouchDesigner's node-based visual programming creates a real-time pipeline where human movement becomes generative art. Multiple creators are independently converging on this stack — from spider-web string simulations to 3D Gaussian splatting to interactive music visualizers.
why_it_matters: This is the democratization of interactive installation art. What used to require a team, custom hardware, and months of C++ now runs on a laptop with a webcam. title: Beyond Prompting: Prompt Architecture as Engineering Discipline
thesis: Prompt engineering is dead. What's replacing it is prompt architecture — the systematic design of context windows, memory layers, retrieval systems, and cognitive scaffolds. The shift from 'write a better prompt' to 'build a better system around the model' is the biggest unlock in practical AI right now.
why_it_matters: Most people are still optimizing individual prompts. The practitioners in these entries have moved past that entirely — they're building systems where the prompt is just one component of a larger architecture. Context management, memory persistence, tool orchestration, and self-correction loops matter more than any single prompt.
action_sketch:
1. Stop optimizing prompts in isolation — map the full context flow
2. Implement RAG with hybrid search + reranking for internal docs
3. Build a memory layer: what the model needs to remember across sessions
4. Add retrieval-augmented generation for domain-specific knowledge
5. Design self-correction: let the model audit its own output
6. Measure: track which context components actually improve output quality
prerequisites: Experience with at least one LLM API

why_it_matters: Everyone's building agents. Most are failing. 1. Start narrow: one task, one tool, one feedback loop
2. Build in guardrails before capability (kill switches, budget limits, scope constraints)
3. Test adversarially: what happens when the agent encounters edge cases?
4. Add persistence: agents need memory to avoid repeating mistakes
5. Monitor: log everything, review regularly, prune bad patterns
6. Scale horizontally: multiple narrow agents > one general agent

title: Skills That Earn Their Lines — benchmark-gated self-editing plus subtraction
thesis: Successor to the harness and second-brain dives. Those stop at 'append a lesson after every mistake'. The catalog now holds the missing machinery — Microsoft SkillOpt rewrites skills only when a benchmark improves, bilevel autoresearch adds a coach loop over the worker, Prime Agent rewrites its own harness to 95.5% on ARC-AGI-3 — and, crucially, evidence that subtraction matters as much as addition: Boris Cherny's simple mode and the setup-purge post show stale rules make newer models dumber. Combine them into a ratchet that both adds and deletes rules, keeping only edits that beat a held-out eval.
why_it_matters: Every power user's CLAUDE.md grows monotonically until it is a tax on every call. A two-way, eval-gated ratchet turns rule accretion into measured improvement, and the winning traces become fine-tuning data you can push into a small local model with Soup.
action_sketch:
Export your last 3 months of Claude history, have a small model tag 40 representative tasks with pass/fail criteria — that is your held-out eval
Run an ablation sweep: drop each CLAUDE.md rule and skill one at a time, rerun the eval, delete anything whose removal does not hurt the score
Add the SkillOpt loop on a nightly cron — skills log issues, an optimizer proposes edits, only score-improving edits merge; export passing traces for a Soup fine-tune later
Falsifier: if eval scores vary more between two identical runs than between best and worst rule sets, your eval is too noisy and the whole ratchet is optimizing noise
prerequisites: A CLAUDE.md and skills folder with some history
A cheap model for grading (Haiku-class or local)

entries.caption: How to 5x your loop system with Bilevel loops #ai #tech
entries.transcript: Most people don't realize that you can get 5x more efficiency from a loop system by just adding another loop on top. Here's how the bi-level loop system works. If you don't already, Andre Carpethy, one of the co-founders of OpenAI, released a loop engineering system that works when you give AI a goal and it works towards it by itself. It tries to change and test whether the results get better. Keeps it if it did, throws a weight if it didn't, and tries the next idea all automated. But here's a problem nobody noticed. Even good loops have bad habits. AI has instincts about what kinds of ideas to try. It keeps going back over the same instincts over and over even after they stop working. Your loop runs 500 experience, but it's really running the same 10 ideas 50 times. This is a fix that Frontier Lab scientists found out. You just add a second loop on top of the first one. The inner loop is the worker. It keeps running experiments exactly like before while the top loop is the coach. The coach does not do any of the work. Its only job is to watch the worker. The coach in the outer loop rewrites the worker's playbook, changing the way it searches for ideas and then setting it back in. Researchers tested this on the same exact benchmark that Carpethy used, and this new Tula version scored five times better than a single loop with the same exact LLM models. The entire improvement came from the structure that one AI is forcing the other AI to explore ideas that normally its instincts would have skipped. entries.transcript: Nobody has talked about this, but someone just built a self-improving and a trading system that literally rewrites its own code whenever it loses money. Top hedge funds spend millions of dollars a year hiring quant traders to research, test, and tweak trading strategies. This setup turns that entire cycle into an automated loop. First, describe the trading idea and the agent translate your rules into clean code, hooks up your broker API, and runs a five-year market stress test in seconds.
